cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.q: A developer accepts Cursor Tab's first suggestion on reflex without reading it, and a bug in an unhandled edge case (like a zero interest rate) surfaces in code review instead. What does the lesson say this mistake costs?
options: Nothing — Tab suggestions are pre-verified
It only matters on the Hobby plan
The bug is caught late, in review, instead of at write time when it was cheap to catch
It voids your Cursor subscription
cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.why: Accepting suggestions on reflex without reading them means bugs surface in review instead of at write time, per the lesson's common mistakes.

cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.q: Why does the lesson recommend writing a short comment stating inputs, outputs, and edge cases before letting Tab generate a function body?
options: Comments are required by Cursor's terms of service
The quality of what you type first sets the ceiling for what Tab can suggest, and naming edge cases up front prevents plausible-looking but wrong completions
It disables ghost-text so you can type manually
It automatically writes unit tests
cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.why: Tab predicts from surrounding context, so a comment stating the contract (including edge cases) raises the ceiling of what it can correctly suggest.

cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.q: A developer on the Hobby tier assumes their Tab completions are lower quality than a paid plan's. What does the lesson say about this?
options: The underlying models are the same on Hobby and paid tiers — only how much usage you get before hitting a cap differs
Hobby tier suggestions intentionally omit edge-case handling
Hobby tier only works with JavaScript
Paid plans use a fundamentally different completion model
cop-b1-setup-and-quality-completions.why: The lesson explicitly corrects this assumption: only usage limits differ between Hobby and paid tiers, not suggestion quality.

cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.q: A developer keeps unrelated files from a different feature open while working on a new one, and Tab's suggestions keep drifting toward that other feature's patterns. What's the fix per the lesson?
options: Turn off Tab and write the code manually
Add more comments to override the pattern
Restart the editor
Close the irrelevant tabs — open and recently edited files are weighted more heavily than the rest of the index
cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.why: Tab weighs open and recently edited files more heavily, so closing unrelated tabs stops it from pulling suggestions toward the wrong pattern.

cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.q: Why does the lesson say a JSDoc block with concrete @example input/output pairs works better than a paragraph of prose description?
options: Worked examples pin down the exact input/output shape, leaving no room to guess wrong on formatting, while prose still leaves decisions ambiguous
JSDoc is the only format Tab can parse
Prose comments are ignored by Tab entirely
Examples reduce the number of tokens used
cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.why: Concrete worked examples remove formatting ambiguity (like currency conversion and symbol placement) that a prose description would still leave open.

cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.q: A developer keeps retyping the same 'always use our ApiResult wrapper' reminder in comment after comment across many files. What does the lesson recommend instead?
options: Keep retyping it — comments are the only way to steer Tab
Write it once as a `.cursor/rules/*.mdc` file so it applies automatically without retyping it every time
Rename every function to include 'ApiResult' in the name
Disable Tab for that project
cop-b2-steer-completions-with-comments-a.why: The lesson explicitly recommends moving a repeated reminder into a standing Rule file instead of retyping it in every comment.

cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.q: A developer asks 'what does this code do?' with nothing selected or referenced. What's the likely result, per the lesson?
options: A precise, verifiable answer about the exact function of concern
An error, since a selection is required
A vague answer instead of an explanation of the specific part they actually care about
An automatic fix applied to the code
cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.why: Asking a generic question with nothing selected or referenced is a named common mistake that produces a vague answer instead of a targeted one.

cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.q: Why does the lesson say to treat an AI explanation of code as a hypothesis rather than a verified fact?
options: Explanations are randomly generated
Neither tool can read selected code accurately
This only applies to the free tier
Either tool can misread control flow just like a human skimming quickly, so it needs verifying against the actual code
cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.why: The lesson explicitly warns that either tool can misread control flow, so explanations should be verified rather than trusted outright.

cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.q: A developer needs to trace a bug across several files before a big refactor. What does the lesson recommend over a quick question in Cursor Chat?
options: Opening a dedicated Claude Code session, since a genuine standalone investigation is better suited to it than a quick in-editor chat
Skipping investigation and guessing at the fix
Asking the same one-line question repeatedly until it's right
Switching to a different programming language
cop-i1-copilot-chat-explanation-and-expl.why: The lesson distinguishes a quick in-editor question from a genuine standalone investigation, recommending a dedicated Claude Code session for the latter.

cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.q: A developer approves an entire multi-file agent diff at once without reading each file individually. What risk does the lesson highlight?
options: The change will fail to compile
This is exactly how scope creep and unrelated changes slip into a commit unnoticed
Agent mode requires per-file approval anyway, so nothing changes
It only affects test files
cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.why: Approving a whole multi-file diff at once without reading each file is the lesson's top-listed way scope creep slips in unnoticed.

cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.q: Why does the lesson recommend naming the exact files that are in bounds when giving any of the three agents a task?
options: It's required syntax for agent mode to run at all
It speeds up the agent's response time
Without it, the agent may 'helpfully' touch a shared utility, config file, or the database schema you didn't want changed
It reduces the number of test cases generated
cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.why: Not naming files or directories that are off-limits is a named common mistake that lets the agent reach into unintended files.

cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.q: A task is delegated to an unattended Codex cloud task, but it turns out to be genuinely ambiguous partway through. What does the lesson warn?
options: The wrong turn is only discovered once the task has already finished, since you can't redirect it mid-course
Codex automatically pauses and asks for clarification
This is fine as long as CI passes
Unattended tasks always fail safely on ambiguity
cop-i2-edit-across-files-with-copilot.why: The lesson explains that unattended surfaces can't be redirected mid-course, so an ambiguous task's wrong turn surfaces only once it's finished.

cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.q: A team lead writes a GitHub issue that just says 'add rate limiting' and delegates it to a Codex cloud task. What does the lesson predict?
options: The task will ask clarifying questions before starting
The task will refuse the issue as underspecified
The PR will exactly match what was needed
The PR will likely solve a different, more generic version of the problem than the one actually intended
cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.why: Writing the issue as a one-line request is a named common mistake that produces a PR solving a more generic version of the problem.

cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.q: Why does the sample issue template include an explicit 'Out of scope' line?
options: It stops the agent from 'helpfully' expanding the task into something bigger and harder to review
It's required metadata for GitHub Issues
It tells the agent which repository to use
It disables CI checks on the resulting PR
cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.why: The 'out of scope' line matters as much as the scope line — it prevents the agent from expanding the task into something harder to review.

cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.q: A reviewer approves an agent-authored PR faster than usual, reasoning that 'the AI already checked it.' What does the lesson say about this?
options: This is the correct approach since agent PRs are pre-verified
The agent did not check business context only a human reviewer has, so the same review rigor as a human contributor's PR still applies
Agent PRs should get less scrutiny only on small repos
This is fine as long as CI passes
cop-a1-coding-agent-issue-to-pull-reques.why: The lesson explicitly warns against reviewing agent-authored PRs less critically — the agent did not check business context only the reviewer has.

cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.q: A developer requests review on a large, high-risk PR with no specific focus. What does the lesson say to expect?
options: A deep, exhaustive security audit automatically
An instant review, since agentic review is always fast
A pass that reads more like a generic style check than a deep analysis of the risks that actually matter
A refusal, since focus areas are mandatory
cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.why: Requesting review with no specific focus on a large PR is a named common mistake, producing a pass that reads more like a style check.

cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.q: A team merges a PR touching authentication logic based solely on an approving AI review, with no human reviewer. What mistake does this match?
options: Verifying a flagged issue by checking the code path
Dismissing a false positive with a reasoning comment
Tracking how much a deeper review pass costs
Treating an approving AI review as equivalent to human sign-off on a change touching security or business logic
cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.why: The lesson explicitly requires pairing AI review with a human reviewer for anything touching business logic, security, or public APIs.

cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.q: A repo runs Codex review on every PR, and separately someone runs Claude Code review at a high effort level. What does the lesson say to watch?
options: Nothing — both are always free
Usage, since a deeper agentic review pass costs more than a quick scan and can add up on an active repo
Only the number of comments left, not any cost
The color scheme of the review comments
cop-a2-ai-code-review-on-github.why: The lesson notes that a deeper agentic review pass costs more than a quick one, so usage is worth watching on an active team repository.

cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.q: A team writes an AGENTS.md that just says 'write clean code' and 'use meaningful names.' Why does the lesson say this fails to change behavior?
options: Generic instructions files are ignored by all three tools entirely
Generic advice doesn't disambiguate anything — it doesn't state repo-specific facts that override default guesses
The file needs to be renamed to CONTRIBUTING.md
Instructions files only work with chat, not completions
cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.why: Generic best-practice advice doesn't change behavior because it doesn't disambiguate anything, unlike specific, repo-true statements.

cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.q: The example AGENTS.md names concrete files like ApiResult<T> and AppError instead of describing conventions abstractly. Why does this matter?
options: File paths are required syntax for the file to parse
It reduces the file's total length
Pointing at concrete files is what lets a model actually apply the convention rather than approximate it
It's only relevant to Codex, not Claude Code or Cursor
cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.why: Pointing at real files instead of describing conventions abstractly is what lets a model apply the rule concretely instead of approximating it.

cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.q: A team maintains three separate hand-written instructions files — one per tool — and they've drifted out of sync. What does the lesson say the fix is?
options: Delete all three and rely on default suggestions
Write one canonical AGENTS.md, since Codex and Cursor read it natively, and import it into CLAUDE.md with `@AGENTS.md` instead of maintaining three separate files
Pick whichever file is newest and delete the other two without comparing them
Ask each tool vendor to standardize on a single format first
cop-a3-custom-instructions-for-your-repo.why: The lesson's core recommendation is one canonical AGENTS.md, read natively by Codex and Cursor and imported into CLAUDE.md, instead of three drifting files.

cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.q: Developers on a team each default to whichever AI coding tool they personally prefer, with no stated policy. What does the lesson say results from this?
options: Nothing — individual preference is always fine for a team
The team ends up with three inconsistent sets of conventions since nobody agreed on which tool is the default for which kind of work
Usage costs automatically balance across the three tools
This is required by each tool's terms of service
cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.why: The lesson's first common mistake is never writing the default-tool policy down, leading to three inconsistent sets of conventions.

cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.q: Why does the sample team policy restrict which repos a Codex cloud task or Claude Code background session can touch?
options: It's a legal requirement for Team/Business plans
Without an access policy, an unattended agent has the same reach into a sensitive repo as into a low-risk one
It reduces the number of PRs opened
It disables human review entirely
cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.why: The lesson explicitly warns that skipping the access-policy line gives an unattended session the same reach into sensitive repos as low-risk ones.

cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.q: Three separate subscriptions — Claude, ChatGPT/Codex, and Cursor — each meter usage differently. What does the lesson say to do about this?
options: Ignore it, since a spike in one always shows up in the others
Cancel two of the three subscriptions to simplify billing
Review usage across all three monthly, since a spike in one doesn't show up in the others
Only the org administrator needs to know usage numbers
cop-a4-integrating-copilot-into-a-team-w.why: The lesson recommends a monthly review across all three separate billing surfaces, since each meters differently and a spike in one won't appear in the others.
